newsitem.title: UK: UK M4 slowdown seen easing rate pressure slightly.
newsitem.headline: UK M4 slowdown seen easing rate pressure slightly.

text.p: A slowdown in British broad money supply growth in April may take the pressure off for a near-term interest rate rise, but with the Bank of England now free to set monetary policy, economists are taking nothing for granted.

"The deceleration of monetary growth will be of some comfort to the authorities," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc. "But it's early days yet to say that broad money aggregates are on a long-term slowing trend."

M4 grew by 10.4 percent in the year to April, still well above the three-to-nine percent monitoring range adopted by the previous government but far below the 11.3 percent growth economists were forecasting for last month.

Shaw said part of the slowdown in monetary growth was due to a surprise surplus on the government's finances in April. Figures out earlier this week showed Britain repaid 36 million pounds of debt last month.

Most analysts expected a public sector deficit of at least one billion pounds in the first month of the financial year. "The PSBR numbers were far better than expected. Some of the slowdown in M4 should be attributed to the negative contribution from the public finances," Shaw said.
Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers, said the money supply figures were softer than expected but agreed that the PSBR was the major factor.
"You would have to see a lot more than just one month's figures to start changing ideas about monetary policy," he said.
Britain's new monetary policy committee is due to meet at some point in June. The Bank will have five members on the new nine-strong committee and the Treasury will have no vote.
"Today's figures may ease the pressure for a rate rise a little, but only a little," Shaw said.

Under the previous monetary arrangement, whereby Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke met Bank of England Governor Eddie George each month to discuss interest rates, minutes from the meeting showed the Governor was consistently concerned about broad money growth while Clarke tended to give it less emphasis.

Building Society Association figures released at the same time as the M4 data showed mortgage lending held up well in April. New new mortgages worth 3.314 billion stg were approved in April, up from 3.212 billion in March.
The British Bankers Association said bank mortgage lending rose by 740 million pounds last month, virtually flat to March. "The housing market is recovering but not at an explosive pace," Shaw said.
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica, noted that bank and building society lending within the M4 aggregrate was also soft, at 4.4 billion stg, compared with 4.8 billion in March.
He also said the latest set of monetary minutes for Clarke's last meeting with George, released on Wednesday, showed the Bank reemphasising concerns about broad money supply.
"M4 probably needs to show growth below nine percent for the central bank to feel genuinely comfortable."
But Hawkins thought a June rate rise was unlikely, with Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown due to unveil his budget next month and many economists expecting significant fiscal tightening.

Neil Parker, economist at the Royal Bank of Scotland disagreed. "The pace of monetary growth still indicates a further rate hike is needed and we forecast a 25 basis point hike at the first monetary policy committee meeting."
The latest monetary minutes showed George urged Clarke to tighten policy by a quarter-point in April. Brown, the new Chancellor, did just that just five days into office, early this month.
